attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The paraphrase is faithful. The testable core is causal: models repeat errors because of what they were trained on. The rest is rhetorical framing ('fantastical', 'stolen'), so 'causal' fits better than 'observation'.

contract.note: Reading 'can't help' as a recurring limitation, not certainty, and 'stolen' as unauthorized use is ordinary and fair. Splitting the claim into mechanism, breadth and sourcing parts is reasonable.

evidence.note: TruthfulQA shows earlier models repeating misconceptions learned from text, which fits the mechanism. But it tests older models, not the March 2024 tools, and says nothing about provenance.
OpenAI confirms GPT-4 is pre-trained to predict the next token, which gives the autocomplete analogy a basis. It does not show that errors cannot be avoided.
Adobe's own statement about an image model trained on licensed data. It touches the breadth of the 'stolen' charge, not the language models the passage is about.

reviews.rationale: The evidence partly backs the error mechanism for earlier language models (e1) and the next-token basis (e2). Nothing in the packet establishes unauthorized sourcing at petabyte scale for the tools discussed, or traces specific training errors into their outputs. Adobe (e3) is a self-disclosure about a different kind of model. The packet does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: A firm 'so will' forecast tied to growing reliance on generative AI. The antecedent is kept and no deadline was stated.

contract.note: Reading 'dependence' as operational reliance and 'dictated' as growing automated influence over what users see is ordinary. Requiring broad evidence before early resolution is fair to an undated forecast.

evidence.note: Google's own statement on the AI Overviews rollout. It shows adoption (the antecedent), not the web-wide outcome.
Microsoft's own statement on the limited rollout of Bing generative search. It shows adoption, and its claim that clicks were maintained cuts against the outcome.
Pew finds fewer clicks when an AI summary appears. It covers Google only, is observational, and does not show a web-wide change.
Preprint published before the evaluation date. It shows AI search expanding and changing which sources users see, but only for search.

reviews.rationale: Adoption appears to be under way (e1, e2, e4), and search-specific studies point toward more automated mediation (e3, e4). No representative evidence shows a web-wide increase caused by AI reliance, so the early-resolution rule is not met. With no deadline, the forecast stays open.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: A firm 'will lead' forecast. It covers both the deployment of generated answers and low-quality content as the reason for it.

contract.note: Keeping the causal commitment matches the speaker's 'will lead'. Requiring evidence of motive is fair, and the contract rightly says another stated benefit does not rule it out.

evidence.note: Google's own announcement shows AI Overviews were deployed in May 2024. It gives no link to low-quality content as the reason.
Google's own statement shows it answered low-quality content with ranking and spam-policy changes. That neither proves nor rules out a further motive for generated answers.

reviews.rationale: Deployment happened (e1), but no evidence ties it to low-quality content, and e2 shows a separate response. Under the contract, deployment alone does not settle the forecast, and with no deadline the missing causal evidence does not count as failure.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post. The quoted promise belongs to Google and is not his claim.

semantics.note: The revision keeps his 'severely doubt' wording. This is graded confidence, not a firm commitment, about a vague 'meaningful' change with no measure or time window.

contract.note: The contract correctly declines to set a probability or materiality threshold, since doing so would rewrite the claim.

evidence.note: Google reports its own 45% figure, combining the March update with earlier work. It is not an independent finding.
A practitioner study finds changed result characteristics, such as word count. It does not measure whether results got meaningfully better.

reviews.rationale: 'Severely doubt' is a statement of probability, and 'meaningfully changes' has no measure or window, so the claim is not scored. The evidence (Google's own figures and a practitioner study) is context only.
